sources.title: Ignacy Łukasiewicz (Q28978), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-24): instance of human, English label 'Ignacy Łukasiewicz', English description 'Polish pharmacist and petroleum industry pioneer (1822-1882)', Korean label 이그나치 루카시에비치, born 1822 (8 and 23 March both recorded), died 7 January 1882, citizenship recorded as Austrian Empire and Austria-Hungary. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Encyclopedia of World Biography (Gale), 'Lukasiewicz, Ignacy' (reproduced on Encyclopedia.com; read in full). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: calls him the inventor of the kerosene lamp and an important figure in the early European oil industry; tells the 1852 distillation work with the lab assistant Jan Zeh (and notes that the relative contributions of the two are a matter of historical dispute), the lamp lit in the Lwów hospital on 31 July 1853, the oil field at Bóbrka developed from the mid-1850s with Tytus Trzecieski (hand-dug wells of 15 m, then 60 m, then 150 m), the refineries and the Chorkówka estate, the end of his pharmacy career in the early 1860s, his funding of schools, churches and roads, the papal order of 1873 and his death of pneumonia on 7 January 1882. Says he had no education in geology or mining and worked 'on an accurate instinct'. Reference-work biography, admiring in tone, partly drawn from Polish institutional web pages.

Piotr Krzywiec, 'The Birth of the Modern Oil Industry in the Northern Carpathians', AAPG Explorer, January 2018, pp. 20-25 (professional geology magazine; read in full from the author's PDF; the author is a geologist and historian of geology at the Polish Academy of Sciences). Independent professional voice: places the birth of the modern oil industry in the mid-19th century as an example of 'parallel thinking' (Abraham Gesner refined kerosene from coal at about the same time), credits the lamp to Łukasiewicz, Jan Zeh and the tinsmith Adam Bratkowski (first used in a Lwów hospital on 31 July 1853), says the Bóbrka mine of 1854 (with Trzecieski and Klobassa) moved from hand-dug wells to percussion drilling and then steam-powered cable-tool drilling and is among the first modern producing oil fields, that he had interests in many later fields and refineries, that he co-organised the first Oil Industry Congress in 1877 which led to the National Oil Society, that he financed participants of the 1863 rising, gave to charity and received the papal honours of 1873, and died a rich man. Magazine essay, short, admiring but not nationalist in framing.

Marek Kępa, 'Ignacy Łukasiewicz: The Generous Inventor of the Kerosene Lamp', Culture.pl (Adam Mickiewicz Institute, October 2021; read in full). Biographical article built on quotations from the biographers Józef Zbigniew Sozański (2004) and Włodzimierz Bonusiak (2007) and on a Polish Radio talk by the historian Andrzej Notkowski: a colleague's 1841 remark that he was 'taciturn, tenacious and extremely hard working', the pharmacist's training and 1850-52 university studies, the 1852 oil analysis and lamp (first documented use March 1853), the move to Gorlice, the Bóbrka mine started by the end of 1854, the 1856 refinery, the 1859 railway kerosene contract, the near-withdrawal after the death of his daughter and a refinery fire, steam drilling after consulting experts, the workers' fund (3 percent of wages for sickness relief, fire relief and family pensions), schools and church funding, the 1877-81 Galician Diet and subsidies for exploratory drilling and geological maps. Flags the Rockefeller visit as legend. Popular article drawing on one family of Polish biographies; admiring.

Piotr Bejrowski, 'Ignacy Łukasiewicz: inventor of the kerosene lamp and founder of the oil industry', Polish History (Museum of the History of Poland; read in full). Short institutional biography: the 1845-48 imprisonment (unscored), work at the 'Under the Golden Star' pharmacy in Lwów with Jan Zeh, studies in Kraków and Vienna 1850-52, the lamp used in the Lwów hospital on 31 July 1853, the pharmacy lease in Gorlice, the Bóbrka company started on Tytus Trzecieski's initiative with Łukasiewicz as director of the mine for many years, the distillery at Ulaszowice in 1856, exhibition awards in Vienna and Lwów, his own advertising and distribution of products in Kraków, Tarnów and Warsaw, drilling improvements up to steam rigs and 240 m, the 'Bracka' fund as one of the first worker insurance systems in Poland, schools and roads, and the 1877 oil congress and National Oil Society. Quotes a remark attributed to him ('this liquid is the country's future wealth'). Institutional, admiring.

Anna Kozicka-Kołaczkowska, "That's oil!... The Apothecary and the Blood of the Earth", Energy Policy Studies no. 1(9), 2022, pp. 19-27 (journal article; read in full from the PDF). Draws on the pharmacy historian Wojciech Roeske and on 19th-century accounts: that he first saw crude oil in June 1852, fractionated it with Zeh (a Vienna privilege of 2 December 1853 names both), his own recorded remarks from an 1871 interview about lamp explosions and his visits to the tinsmith Bratkowski, the Austrian chemist Hans Gintl's 1873 account that in 1853-54 he sent distillate samples and lamps to Vienna (to the factory owner Heindl and to Professor Redtenbacher) and to Paris to find capital and attention but found no interest in Galicia, a report that the Liebig Institute in Munich had dismissed the Bóbrka oil as 'fat without value', the 1864 Ditmar patent of the burner without agreement with him, his training of mining personnel at Bóbrka, and later accounts of high-quality kerosene. Partisan in tone (a pharmacy-history argument for his primacy); the author is a philologist and editor, so the factual layer rests on the cited historians.

Museum of the Oil and Gas Industry named after Ignacy Łukasiewicz in Bóbrka, 'A few facts about Łukasiewicz' (museum web page; read in full). Museum-owned biography: studies and pharmacy work, the 1852-53 research with Jan Zeh in the back room of the Lwów pharmacy, the first lamps made by the tinsmith Adam Bratkowski and lit on 31 July 1853, the move to Gorlice, the Bóbrka company founded in 1854 with Tytus Trzecieski, the 1856 Ulaszowice distillery, prizes at exhibitions in Jasło, Lwów and Vienna, the hand rig of 1862 and steam rigs, the attempt to found a mining school, the 'Kasa Bracka' insurance system for employees, the papal order of 1873 and his death on 7 January 1882. Self-interested (the museum is his memorial) and short; used only for consistent dates and facts.

Jerzy Pilecki, 'Ignacy Łukasiewicz: założenia i problemy przygotowywanej monografii', Kwartalnik Historii Nauki i Techniki 2(1), 1957, pp. 95-118 (Polish Academy of Sciences quarterly; read in part, in Polish: the figure caption, the opening argument and the passage on his field research; the remainder was not read). Historian's outline of a planned monograph, written in the 1950s with a strongly social-reformist framing. Useful for: the 1957 caption identifying the 1884 portrait as Andrzej Grabowski's portrait of Łukasiewicz (then owned by the Krosno district council and held by the Central Oil Office in Warsaw); the author's comparison, citing contemporary writers (Szajnocha, Szczepanowski, Windakiewicz), of Bóbrka's working conditions with the speculation of Borysław; the social insurance introduced from 1866 at the Bóbrka mine and the Chorkówka refinery; and his field recovery of the two 'brotherhood' cash boxes of the mine and refinery.

experimentation.rationale: [src_lukasiewicz_wb, src_lukasiewicz_eps, src_lukasiewicz_aapg, src_lukasiewicz_bobrka | 1852-1862 | reference biography, journal article, professional magazine, museum page] Two families of evidence: the 1852-53 laboratory and lamp trials (night-long trials that 'more than once ended in small explosions', in the Gale biography; his own 1871 remark that a lamp tank ignited and almost burned him and that he went to the tinsmith to 'try and improve', as quoted in the journal article) and the later field trials at Bóbrka, where the mine moved from hand-dug wells to hand percussion drilling and then to steam cable-tool drilling (AAPG, museum page). SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 76 / 0.62 to 72 / 0.58 because the lamp-trial details rest on his own recollection and one encyclopedia, and credit for the distillation is shared with Zeh and disputed.

persistence.rationale: [src_lukasiewicz_eps, src_lukasiewicz_culture, src_lukasiewicz_aapg, src_lukasiewicz_wb | 1853-1861 | journal article, popular biography article, professional magazine, reference biography] The Austrian chemist Gintl (1873, quoted in the journal article) records that in 1853-54 he sent samples and lamps to Vienna and Paris to find capital and attention after no interest could be raised in Galicia, 'without the desired success'; he kept working as a pharmacist while pursuing the oil (journal article, Gale); after the death of his daughter and a refinery fire he considered withdrawing but was dissuaded and continued (Culture.pl, from his biographers); the AAPG essay credits the Carpathian industry to his hard work and persistence. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 78 / 0.64 to 74 / 0.60 because the sample-sending episode is one independent contemporary witness retold by one author, and the reconsideration after bereavement rests on one biographer.

proactive_agency.rationale: [src_lukasiewicz_culture, src_lukasiewicz_aapg, src_lukasiewicz_mhp, src_lukasiewicz_wb | 1853-1880 | popular biography article, professional magazine, institutional biography, reference biography] Several separately documented self-started moves: he left Lwów at the turn of 1853-54 to lease a pharmacy in Gorlice near the oil area and continued the work there; in 1854 he and Trzecieski and Klobassa started the Bóbrka mine; he co-organised the 1877 Oil Industry Congress, which led to the National Oil Society (AAPG, Polish History); and he lobbied the Galician Diet for subsidies for exploratory drilling and geological maps (Culture.pl). Four sources, mostly from the Polish institutional tradition, agree on these acts. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 78 / 0.64 to 76 / 0.62 because the Diet-lobbying claim rests on one historian quoted by one article.

opportunity_sensing.rationale: [src_lukasiewicz_wb, src_lukasiewicz_aapg, src_lukasiewicz_eps | 1852-1877 | reference biography, professional magazine, journal article] The Gale biography says he acted on an 'accurate instinct' that petroleum would prove immensely important; the AAPG essay says he had a far-reaching vision of oil developing Galicia and organised professional exchange early; the journal article reports that he sought outside capital for the new fuel in Vienna and Paris. The same AAPG essay calls the birth of the industry an example of 'parallel thinking' (others reached kerosene independently). SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 74 / 0.58 to 70 / 0.52 because the foresight is described retrospectively by reference writers, not shown in a contemporary document, and the other sources are partisan or short.

analytical_rigor.rationale: [src_lukasiewicz_eps, src_lukasiewicz_culture, src_lukasiewicz_wb | 1852-1860s | journal article, popular biography article, reference biography] The pharmacy historian Roeske (quoted in the journal article) holds that the fractional distillation was done by laboratory scientific method, with a fraction between 250 and 350 degrees Celsius found to burn evenly, and the radio historian Notkowski (via Culture.pl) calls it the first methodical, laboratory-scientific distillation of oil; Culture.pl adds that he later consulted geology and drilling experts. The Gale biography instead calls him an amateur inventor without education in geology or mining. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 66 / 0.52 strong inference to 58 / 0.44 inference because both favourable accounts repeat one Polish pharmacy-history thesis, and a reference biography describes him differently.

resourcefulness.rationale: [src_lukasiewicz_wb, src_lukasiewicz_culture, src_lukasiewicz_aapg | 1853-1870s | reference biography, popular biography article, professional magazine] The mine began as a ditch (reported as 100 or 120 m long and about 1.2 m deep) in which oil skimmed from water was gathered; the first wells were dug with picks and shovels and timbered, then deepened from 15 m to 60 m and then 150 m (Gale), and drilling later used a steam engine after he consulted specialists (Culture.pl, AAPG); the first lamps were built with a local tinsmith. Three sources from different traditions describe the progression from minimal means; the source families are reasonably independent, so no concentration lowering was applied.

collaboration.rationale: [src_lukasiewicz_aapg, src_lukasiewicz_wb, src_lukasiewicz_culture, src_lukasiewicz_eps | 1852-1877 | professional magazine, reference biography, popular biography article, journal article] He worked with Zeh and the tinsmith Bratkowski on the lamp, founded the Bóbrka enterprise with Trzecieski and Klobassa and formed a company with them around 1861, co-organised the first oil congress, and trained mining staff and received visiting oilmen at Bóbrka. The Gale biography notes that the relative contributions of the two pharmacists are a matter of historical dispute. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 68 / 0.54 to 64 / 0.50 because the partnership details repeat one institutional narrative, the Zeh relationship is contested, and the claim that he advised competitors is an editorial remark in a popular article.

impact_motivation.rationale: [src_lukasiewicz_culture, src_lukasiewicz_kwartalnik, src_lukasiewicz_mhp, src_lukasiewicz_bobrka, src_lukasiewicz_aapg | 1860s-1880 | popular biography article, academy quarterly, institutional biography, museum page, professional magazine] He financed schools (including girls' schools and a lace-making school), roads, bridges and churches; from 1866 or 1868 the Bóbrka mine and Chorkówka refinery carried a workers' insurance fund (sickness care, relief after fires, family pensions) funded by 3 percent of wages; and contemporary inspectors cited in the 1957 article rated his enterprises among the best-run in the country in contrast with Borysław. The papal honour of 1873 was for his charity. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 76 / 0.60 to 72 / 0.56 because most of the material is institutional or memorial in origin, the 1957 reading is ideological, and the Rockefeller-visit story is legend and not used.

risk_tolerance.rationale: [src_lukasiewicz_eps, src_lukasiewicz_wb, src_lukasiewicz_culture | 1854-1861 | journal article, reference biography, popular biography article] He left a post at a leading Lwów pharmacy for a leased pharmacy in Gorlice and began mining in 1854 although, in the account based on his own 1871 interview, a Munich institute had judged the oil 'fat without value'; he invested in many shafts. But he kept working as a pharmacist until the early 1860s while the field was proven, which is a hedge, and he nearly withdrew after a refinery fire and a bereavement. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 62 / 0.48 to 58 / 0.44 because the Munich assay story is from his own telling and the evidence of hedging cuts the other way.

mastery_orientation.rationale: [src_lukasiewicz_wb, src_lukasiewicz_culture, src_lukasiewicz_mhp, src_lukasiewicz_eps | 1836-1870s | reference biography, popular biography article, institutional biography, journal article] He trained through years of apprentice and assistant pharmacy work, then took a leave from his post in 1850-52 for university pharmacy studies in Kraków and Vienna (Gale, Culture.pl, Polish History), and afterwards kept improving the refining of kerosene for years, winning awards at exhibitions in Vienna and Lwów (Polish History, journal article). SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 66 / 0.52 to 64 / 0.50 because the exhibition awards are reported by memorial and partisan sources.

portrait.source: Oil portrait of Ignacy Łukasiewicz by Andrzej Grabowski (1833-1886), dated 1884, i.e. two years after the sitter's death; Wikimedia Commons file 'Ignacy Lukasiewicz.jpg' (356 x 486 pixels, used unchanged, no upscaling, no crop). Sitter identification: the figure caption in Jerzy Pilecki, Kwartalnik Historii Nauki i Techniki 1957 (Polish Academy of Sciences) reads 'Portret Ignacego Łukasiewicza ... wykonany w 1884 r. przez Andrzeja Grabowskiego', owned then by the Krosno district council and held by the Central Oil Office in Warsaw; the same portrait is used by Culture.pl, Polish History and as the Wikidata main image. The present holder was not found.
portrait.license: Public domain by age: the painter Andrzej Grabowski died in 1886 (well over 70 years), so the work is out of copyright in Poland and in the United States; no institutional holder terms exist to apply (the present holder was not identified and the 1957 record names only the then owners)
portrait.attribution: Andrzej Grabowski, portrait of Ignacy Łukasiewicz, oil on canvas, 1884. A posthumous painting made two years after the sitter's death, not a lifetime likeness; whether it was based on life sketches or a photograph is not documented. Image via Wikimedia Commons, public domain.
portrait.creator: Andrzej Grabowski (1833-1886)

provenance.notes: portrait_preflight: PLAUSIBLE (Stage B) / lead SURVIVED: the Commons file of Andrzej Grabowski's 1884 portrait was re-checked and used unchanged (356 x 486). No holder record for the painting exists online that I could find: the only holder trace is the 1957 Pilecki article caption (then owned by the Krosno district council, held by the Central Oil Office in Warsaw), which also independently confirms the sitter and the painter and date. Rights basis is age only (painter died 1886); no institutional terms apply because no current holder was identified. A bounded retry for a lifetime photograph (Commons category of 26 files, Polish Wikipedia images, Polona API not available, web searches of the National Digital Archive and National Museum catalogues) found none that is rights-clear; Culture.pl shows an agency photograph (Forum) that is not open. Nationality PL (Wikidata lists the Austrian Empire and Austria-Hungary as citizenship; this is the usual national classification of a Galician Pole). KO NAME: 이그나치 루카시에비치 is both the Korean Wikipedia title and the Wikidata Korean label (authoritative-label class). ATTRIBUTION: attributable (extensive documentary trail from the 1850s and a rich later biography). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: Gale Encyclopedia of World Biography entry (src_lukasiewicz_wb). READ (7 sources besides Wikidata): Gale entry (full), AAPG Explorer essay by Krzywiec (full), Culture.pl article (full), Polish History essay (full), Kozicka-Kołaczkowska journal article (full), Bóbrka museum page (full), Pilecki 1957 article (partly). Wikipedia not used. Not opened: Sozański 2004, Bonusiak, Roeske, Brzozowski, Gintl 1873 (all via secondary quotation only), the Polish Biographical Dictionary entry, Polish Radio. PERSPECTIVES: (1) reference biography (Gale), (2) independent geologist-historian (AAPG), (3) popular article on Polish biographies (Culture.pl), (4) museum-institutional biographies (Polish History, Bóbrka), (5) partisan pharmacy-history journal piece, (6) 1957 academy article with a social-reformist reading. NON-SELF BEHAVIOURAL SOURCES: Gale, AAPG, Culture.pl, the journal article's quotation of the Austrian chemist Gintl (a contemporary non-Polish witness), the 1957 article's citation of contemporary inspectors. Self-report: his 1871 interview, as quoted by the journal article. CONTRADICTIONS AND LIMITS: credit for the distillation between Łukasiewicz and Zeh is disputed (Gale says so; the Vienna privilege names both); the AAPG essay notes parallel invention (Gesner); sources give the lamp's first use as March 1853 (pharmacy window) or 31 July 1853 (hospital) and the Bóbrka start as 1854 or 'by the end of 1854'; the tinsmith is Adam or Andrzej Bratkowski; the Gale entry says he was an uneducated amateur whereas pharmacy historians stress his training; the Rockefeller visit is legend; the workers' fund is dated 1866 or 1868; 'world's first' mine and refinery claims are not repeated as fact. POLITICS: his youthful conspiratorial activity, two arrests and funding of the 1863 rising, and his Galician Diet seat 1877-81, are context only and unscored (primary identity is pharmacist, inventor and oil industrialist). MAJOR ACHIEVEMENT GATE: PASS (cards: kerosene and lamp, the Bóbrka field and refineries, building the industry through the 1877 congress and society).
